source_span: there are credible reasons why investors risk underestimating the scale of the tightening ahead... markets tend to underestimate, rather than overestimate the extent of hiking cycles
source_chain: Central banks are overcorrecting for being 'too late' in 2021-23 (a more hawkish reaction function than last cycle, per Fed Chair Warsh's own 'more than five years above target' remark) and financial conditions remain looser than in 2022, therefore more hiking is needed than markets assume, therefore every prior cycle (1994: 140bp priced vs 300bp delivered full-year; 2022: 200bp priced vs 400bp+ delivered) shows markets systematically underprice the scale of tightening at the start, therefore investors should expect this cycle to go further than currently priced. No explicit invalidation level is given — the argument rests on historical pattern and structural reaction-function analysis, not a market price threshold.
pulse_chain: The Fed's first hike in three years reframes the question from 'when do cuts start' to 'how many more hikes land,' therefore futures pricing ~75bp more by next June (DB) is likely too low because markets have underpriced every prior cycle the same way (1994: 300bp vs 140bp priced; 2022: 400bp vs 200bp priced, both DB) and because a Fed 'late last time' overcorrects into a more hawkish reaction function this time (mirrors DB's Warsh-overcorrection point), therefore Goldman's dovish 'one more hike then flat' case fails because it needs cooperating data and instead core PCE surprised higher on an oil shock (Saudi strikes) feeding straight into rates (Cboe's 65% 10Y-oil correlation), therefore rates run higher for longer. Invalidation: a decisive 10Y close above 5% before the Oct 27-28 FOMC, with BTIG's 4.92% cited as the level that flips the yield uptrend.
why: The pulse carries DB's specific causal skeleton — the historical underpricing pattern with matching 1994/2022 figures and the reaction-function-overcorrection argument (echoing DB's Warsh quote) — in the same direction and correctly attributed to Deutsche Bank, and supplements it with a properly-sourced BTIG invalidation level rather than inventing one or reversing any DB step.
